title: Early seasonal error scales improved mean sea-level log scores at four West Coast gauges in 1990-2024
abstract: Two error scales, learned from early prediction errors, gave better later mean log scores than one scale. We tested monthly mean sea level at San Diego, San Francisco, Astoria and Seattle. The scales used only errors from 1975-1989. The test used 1,649 site-months in 1990-2024. The equal-site mean log score gain was 0.0621 nats per month. The conditional 95% five-year block interval was 0.0430 to 0.0822. Across the four gauges, coverage of 90% intervals changed from 84.0% to 90.3% in October-March and from 96.7% to 90.1% in April-September. These pooled values hide local errors. Seattle warm-half coverage fell to 82.4%. This is a test of uncertainty estimates from revised observations. It does not establish a physical cause or an operational flood forecast.

display.caption: Early seasonal scales improved later log scores at three gauges and reduced pooled seasonal coverage errors. Site intervals are conditional 95% five-year block intervals. Seattle warm-half coverage remained too low.

citations.reason: Published sites, input snapshot, quality rule and local-history design informed this uncertainty test. Observations overlap; no code or fits reused.
